speakeroldname: Hon. J. J. McCann (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
In order to clarify statements
which already have been made and to answer questions asked by several hon. members with reference to television, I wish to make this brief statement.
In my statement of December 8, 1952, I mentioned six centres in which Canadian Broadcasting Corporation television stations are to be established immediately, and indicated that applications would now be received for private stations to serve other areas. I pointed out that under the plan the private stations licensed would carry national program service of the C.B.C., besides having time for programming on their own. I also said, as reported at page 409 of Hansard of December 8, 1952:
Since the objective will be to extend services as widely throughout Canada as is practicable, no two stations will be licensed at the present to serve the same area. A television station can serve only a comparatively small area. Canada is very large and it will require a good many stations before television can be brought to the people in most parts of our country. It is desirable to have one station in as many areas as possible before there are two in any one area.
These words make it clear that it was not the policy of the government to create monopoly in television or to limit any one area indefinitely to one television station.
The principle of one station to an area is to apply only until an adequate national television system is developed. At the rate that applications for stations are now being received it may not be long before there is a sufficient degree of national coverage to justify the government and the C.B.C. giving
consideration to permitting two and perhaps in some cases more than two stations in certain areas. It is anticipated that, in due course, private stations will be permitted in areas covered by C.B.C. stations, and the
C.B.C. may establish stations in some areas originally covered by private stations.
The ultimate objective of the C.B.C. is to have at least one station in every province of Canada where that is practicable. We understand that private applications have been under development in the five provinces where no C.B.C. station is now under way, and the government does not want to discourage immediate establishment in these areas of private stations which will further extend national service coverage. For that reason licences granted for private stations in those provinces will contain a provision that, before establishing a competing station, the C.B.C. will ascertain whether the area is likely to afford adequate financial support for two stations. If not, it may offer to purchase the private station at a fair and reasonable price rather than set up a new one.

In connection with that, may I ask whether the understanding is that the minister would regard an adequate national television service as having been established if there is at least one station in every province.
That is the ultimate objective, and that, along with private stations, will constitute the national coverage.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. Louis S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: DISTINGUISHED VISITORS-THE PREMIER OF FRANCE AND MEMBERS OF HIS CABINET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I believe you will find it fitting that I draw the attention of the house to the presence of the distinguished visitors who have just entered the diplomatic gallery, in company with the French ambassador, His Excellency Mr. Guerin; I refer to the President of the council of ministers of the French Republic, Mr. Rene Mayer, the Minister for Foreign Affairs, Mr. Georges Bidault, and the Minister of Finance, Mr. Maurice Bourges-Maunoury.

It is important that mention be made of this visit in the official record of the House of Commons so that its readers may also be acquainted with the honour bestowed upon us this afternoon by the representatives of France, in thus attending one of our sittings.
It is important too that we say to our distinguished visitors in our capacity as representatives, in this house, of the people of the whole country, that we wish them to carry back from their short visit among us the vivid impression that all Canadians, from coast to coast, wish to carry out in an efficient and fruitful manner their co-operation with our mother countries, as well as with the other European nations, in order to defend this civilization for which we are indebted to them and of which our democratic institutions are an essential expression.
(Text):

maintopic: DISTINGUISHED VISITORS-THE PREMIER OF FRANCE AND MEMBERS OF HIS CABINET
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I join with the Prime Minister in expressing the welcome that is in the heart of every hon. member to the distinguished representatives of France who are with us here this afternoon. To the Prime Minister and his associates may we say that under our democratic system we also have an opposition, and that opposition is part of our democratic procedure. But may I assure them, through you, sir, that in our welcome this afternoon there is certainly complete harmony, complete understanding, and only one thought, and that is to welcome them and to wish that in their high responsibilities they may guide their great nation to the destiny that we all wish it to share in these troubled years ahead. There are deep bonds of affection between our country and France that are not measured alone by the fact that France was one of the two countries from which those races which joined to make a nation came to these shores many years ago.
Then, there is the other point that is of great importance to all Canadians from every part of Canada. Hundreds of thousands of young Canadians came to know France, through the service they gave in a common cause. Many thousands of those Canadians sleep forever in French soil. The hearts of hundreds of thousands of Canadians here in Canada are forever deeply bound to the soil and people of France.
All those who have had the privilege of seeing what has happened in these past few
Welcome to French Officials years have great admiration for the magnificent work that has already been done to rebuild a nation which, for the second time in a single generation, has felt the devastation of war. The recovery of France, its physical rebuilding, and the unity of purpose which has become so apparent is of great advantage not only to France itself, but to the whole free world.
May I say to the distinguished visitors: I join the Prime Minister in the words he used when he said that it was the wish and hope of every Canadian that your cause may be advanced in every way. And I simply join with him in expressing what I know is the hope of every one of us, that the recovery and rebuilding of France may proceed to meet your highest dreams, and that in the years ahead France may take her proper place among the nations of the world in giving leadership to that ideal of civilization which is our common heritage.

Yes, and I am going to explain. The table shows, for instance, that up to February 1, or February 20 in the case of the customs tariff, the customs duty on regular size cigarettes, Camels and Chesterfields for example, imported from the United States, was $2 per pound plus 15 per cent ad valorem, a total of $5.53 cents per thousand cigarettes. The customs duty of $2 per pound is the equivalent of $5 per thousand cigarettes. The ad valorem duty is the equivalent of 53 cents. Then there was an additional duty of $2 per thousand and an excise tax of 2 cents on each 5 cigarettes. If you add the sales tax of $1.10 you get a figure of $12.63 for the total aggregate customs and excise taxes on American cigarettes imported into Canada. The addition of the excise duty, excise tax and sales tax on Canadian cigarettes before the proposed changes give a figure of $10.95 which means that the difference, the protection for the Canadian cigarettes, is $1.68.
In this bill it is proposed to take off the $2 additional duty on imported cigarettes, not only American, and reduce the excise duty on Canadian cigarettes from $6 to $4. The reduction is the same in each case and, consequently, the spread will be the same- $1.68-which will remain the protection in favour of Canadian cigarettes. That means that American cigarettes cannot compete on the market any more now than they could before the proposed changes.
There is a difference with respect to king size cigarettes and that is the reason for the proposed change in the excise duty instead of the excise tax. Up to now there was no additional customs duty on imported king size cigarettes, and the combined customs duty, excise and sales taxes on imported king size cigarettes was $11.98. Because of an excise duty of $11 per thousand on Canadian-made king size cigarettes, had they been manufactured, the aggregate of such excise duties and sales taxes would have been $16.46, which would have given a spread in favour of the American or other imported cigarettes of around $4.50. Therefore, in the proposed changes in the Excise Act, which we will study in a few minutes, the duty will be dropped from $11 to $5. The protection in favour of any Canadian-made king size cigarettes from now on will be $2.12 per thousand.

We are glad to see this very modest reduction in taxes being made. It is a step in the right direction. speechtext:
There was complete
agreement with the proposal made at that time. We all recognize the increasing demands involved in farming operations, particularly arising because of the fact that agricultural operations are constantly becoming more mechanized, and increasing use of the facilities of the Farm Improvement Loans Act is most necessary. In outlining the results achieved since the measure was first introduced in 1944, the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance presented some very interesting figures. They indicated that up to December, 1952, almost one-third of a million loans had been negotiated, totalling $350 million. That is a very remarkable figure.
I think it is also amazing that the total losses guaranteed to the banks and paid by the government only amounted to something like $38,000 over the eight-year period, or an average of $4,800 per year. I think that indicates clearly that generally speaking farmers are very sincere and honest and will always make every effort to meet their obligations when at all possible. In view of the fact that there was only an insignificant loss averaging $4,800 per year over the period of eight years, and in view of what the Farm Improvement Loans Act means to the farmers, while we probably cannot do so in our consideration of the present measure I should like the parliamentary assistant to recommend to the minister and his staff that serious consideration be given to increasing the guarantee to the banks from 10 per cent to 20 per cent, with the understanding that the banks might lower the rate of interest to farmers from 5 per cent to 4 or 4J, per cent.
I know that the minister has studied the matter very carefully in his department and has given it serious thought, but we must remember that today many young people are drifting away from the farms and are not following that occupation. In fact I understand that the average age of farmers today is well up in the fifties. If we are to make full use of the purposes for which these loans were first made, then I think we should give earnest consideration to broadening the terms under which such loans are made. No one realizes more than I that this is a good act. That was pointed out at the resolution stage and we all agree, but I think we can make it a still better act.
Personally I would hesitate to recommend that any young man should commence farming operations today because of the fact that it takes a considerable amount of money to

finance such operations. We have to consider the fact that these loans have helped so many of our farmers considerably. I know personally that they are of great benefit to agriculture, and if we want to help our young people in particular who are starting to farm then I suggest that it would be most acceptable and beneficial if the rate of interest on such loans could be reduced to 4 per cent. The fact that only $4,800 a year has been paid out over a period of eight years indicates that farmers make every effort to repay their loans in full, and I know they will continue to do so. A considerable amount of money running into millions of dollars has been paid out under the agricultural prices support legislation, and I believe that under the terms of the Farm Improvement Loans Act we can give considerable help to our younger farmers. I trust the parliamentary assistant will recommend to his department that serious consideration be given to what I have suggested.

Unfortunately the parliamentary assistant is in a committee and we propose to change the order for that reason.
The main purpose of the bill that is before us today is to extend until August 1, 1957, certain vital sections of the Canadian Wheat Board Act which would otherwise expire at the end of the current crop year. So that hon. members may consider the legislation in its proper perspective, I intend to outline briefly the record of the Canadian wheat board, to review events that have occurred since a similar extension of powers took place in 1950, and to set forth the position as I see it today.
The Canadian' Wheat Board Act was enacted in its original form in 1935. The 1935 legislation empowered the board to accept wheat, to pay a specified price, and to distribute the profits of the board, if any, in the form of participation payments. It was what we nowadays refer to as a voluntary board; a floor price was provided but the farmer could, and from time to time many of them did, sell on the open market rather than to the board.
In September, 1943, to meet wartime emergencies and under the authority of the War Measures Act, all commercial stocks of western wheat were taken over by the crown at the prevailing prices and the wheat board became the sole marketing agency through
Canadian Wheat Board Act which western producers could sell their wheat. This was the beginning of the present system of wheat board marketing. In effect, the board became a wheat pool handling all western wheat, making an initial payment at time of delivery and declaring interim and final payments as the wheat was sold out of the pool.
Until 1947, the wheat board operated under emergency legislation, first the War Measures Act and later the transitional powers act. By that time it had become quite clear that an overwhelming majority of western producers preferred this board method of selling their wheat. Agricultural organizations were unanimously in favour of continuation of the wheat board as the sole marketing agency for western wheat. Accordingly, in 1947, the Canadian Wheat Board Act was amended giving the board the necessary powers to continue marketing wheat as it had been doing since 1943.
So popular, in fact, was this system of marketing wheat that strong representations were made to the government by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture that the system should be applied to western oats and barley. The 1947 legislation enabled this to be done. But because a high proportion of oats and barley is marketed within provincial boundaries, and because we were anxious that the extension of the monopoly powers of the board to these grains should have the full support of provincial legislation and all three provincial legislatures, the government agreed to implement the relevant sections of the act only if the three prairie provinces passed complementary legislation. They did so, and the wheat board commenced the handling of oats and barley on the same basis as wheat on August 1, 1949. Again in 1950 the act came before parliament for another extension and again there could be no doubt whatever of the western farmers' overwhelming support for the prevailing system of handling their wheat, oats and barley. The government had no hesitation in recommending a further extension for three years to July 31, 1953.
A further proof of farm support came in 1951 when a plebiscite was held on the subject of the marketing of oats and barley. Thirty-four thousand farmers in Manitoba voted on this question:
Do you wish to continue to sell your oats and barley as at present-that is, through the board?
A total of 30,622 or 89 per cent voted "Yes".
To many hon. members these are familiar facts. I give them here so that all members may be aware of the continuous support that has been given by western farmers to the
3416	HOUSE OF
Canadian Wheat Board Act present system of grain marketing and why the government has no hesitation whatever in recommending a further extension for four years. It is truly remarkable that in spite of the attacks that have been made from time to time on grain marketing policy, both within this house and elsewhere, the present wheat board method of handling grain continues to be supported so strongly. To me this support indicates that the methods of handling grain which have been followed have met the requirements of the day, and that the members of the wheat board have discharged their duties with a high degree of competence.
' It is not my usual practice to refer to the services of particular public servants, but I should like on this occasion to express a word of appreciation of the great service rendered to the people of this country and in particular to the farmers of western Canada by the chief commissioner of the wheat board, Mr. George Mclvor. Mr. Mclvor has been connected with the board from its beginning, first as sales manager, then as board member and for the past 16 years as chief commissioner. Throughout that period he has discharged his duties with a high degree ol competence and good judgment.
I should also like to express my appreciation of the work of the other members of the board, Mr. W. C. McNamara and Mr. W. Riddel. Both these men came to the board after serving the producers of western Canada in an executive capacity with the Saskatchewan pool elevators, and they brought to the board an invaluable experience in the handling of grain.
The present method of marketing western wheat has been approved on two occasions by parliament: in 1947 and again in 1950. On both occasions it was possible to point to satisfactory operating results, results which returned good prices to the producer. Now, in 1953, over nine years after the wheat board became the sole marketing agency for western wheat, it is appropriate to look back over the record. The striking fact about that record is the high and stable level of returns to producers. In 1943-44 the producer received a total return for No. 1 northern wheat, basis in store Fort William-Port Arthur, of $1.37 per bushel; in 1944-45, $1,434; in the five-year pool period 1945-46 to 1949-50, $1.83; in 1950-51, $1,854; and in 1951-52, $1,834.
In other words from August 1, 1945, to July 31, 1952, a period of seven full crop years, the price realized by the board and paid to the producer was between $1.83 and $1,854 for No. 1 northern, basis in store at the lakehead. When one is looking for reasons why the board method of handling

hon. members are aware, the 1952 crop was the largest ever harvested on the prairies of Canada-664 million bushels of wheat; 346 million bushels of oats, and 281 million bushels of barley. It was a high grade crop. Almost 80 per cent of the wheat will grade No. 3 northern or better. Although the protein content, as might be expected, is a little below average, we are once again able to offer our customers the high grades and heavy weights per bushel which, over the years, they have come to associate with Canadian wheat.
Our problem this crop year is rather different from the problems experienced in the past two years. We have no worries about excess moisture, and low grades do not form an undue proportion of our stocks. Our main problem is to move the grain forward from the farms into position for export. Sales have been excellent, surpassing any previous crop year at this date, and with a little luck I think we shall establish new records for export clearances of grain from Canada, even exceeding the record established in 1951-52 when 509 million bushels were moved out of this country.
I have already mentioned the contribution made to the movement of earlier crops by the transport controller. During the present crop year the value of Mr. Milner's work in co-ordinating the lake and rail facilities of this country has been immeasurable. In spite of the steel strike and its aftermath, grain clearances down the lakes in Canadian vessels during the 1952 season established new records. Deliveries by producers since August 1, 1952, have been greater than in any postwar year.

Although our sales are heavy and our export clearances of record proportions, there will be a big carryover of grain at the end of the current crop season; but this does not necessarily mean that Canada is beginning to accumulate burdensome surpluses. We shall have a big carryover simply because for three years we have harvested extraordinarily large crops and in 1952 raised a crop almost twice normal size. It is a good thing for the world that we did raise big crops, for the world has been especially dependent on North America for essential food supplies. And, if nature is less bountiful in the future, we may be thankful that we have something left over at the present time.
When I was preparing for this debate I came across something I said on April 20, 1950, during the debate on the 1950 amendments to the wheat board act. This is what I said, as reported at page 1734 of Hansard:
One can be either an optimist or a pessimist about the ability of Canada to dispose of her wheat at reasonable prices in the trading world of today. I prefer to be an optimist. In fact, if I were not an optimist at this stage, I would be a poor selection for the minister in charge of our wheat selling organization. I believe that we can sell our surplus wheat at prices that will return a profit to our farmers in the future as we have in the past. The reputation of Canadian wheat is unquestioned in world markets. Under the trading conditions of today, price and quality are not always the determining factor to the extent that they were in prewar days, but price and quality still count for much. Canada has established a reputation in world wheat markets for fair dealing, which will stand us in good stead. The deficit countries of the world will continue to require wheat, and I believe that Canadian wheat will continue to find a market in those countries. The Canadian wheat board has demonstrated its ability to handle Canada's wheat marketing problems efficiently, and I have every confidence that this ability will be further demonstrated in the years to come.
That is the end of the quotation. Perhaps if I had known what was going to happen to our crops in 1950 and 1951 I might not have put myself so clearly on the record as an optimist. In the event, however, optimism was fully justified.
I am still an optimist. I continue to believe that Canada will be able to find markets for her grain at satisfactory prices. I do not mean that the world will beat a path to our door clamouring for our wheat, or that we shall always get the prices we would like to get. What I do believe is that importing countries will require wheat in substantial and growing quantities over the years to come, and that Canada is in a good position to get a share of the market sufficient to dispose of her exportable surpluses at reasonably satisfactory prices.

Hon. members are aware that negotiations are under way for a renewal of the international wheat agreement. You will not expect me to comment at this time on the progress of the negotiations. We hope for a favourable outcome, but we shall not be easily satisfied. It is the government's view that an international wheat agreement can be of benefit to both exporting and importing countries, but if mutually satisfactory terms cannot be agreed upon we can, as we have done in the past, sell our wheat successfully without an agreement. If and when an agreement is signed in Washington, legislation will be presented to parliament to ratify the agreement. The amendments in the present bill are not contingent upon renewal of the international wheat agreement. I have heard suggestions that the continuation of the wheat board in its present form is contingent upon an agreement, but this is not so. The two matters are quite unrelated.
As I said ait the outset, the main purpose of the bill before us is to extend until July 31, 1957, those sections of the act which give the board powers to continue as the sole marketing agency for western wheat, oats and barley. These powers might have been extended indefinitely, but it is the government's view that they ought to come before parliament for review and extension every few years. There are also a few amendments of a more technical nature, including one to close out old and inactive crop accounts.
The government has received a number of suggestions regarding use of these unclaimed funds for which no owner can be discovered. As none of the suggestions seem to meet with general approval, it has been decided that funds that have been unclaimed for six years or more will be transferred to a separate wheat board account to be used for such purposes as the governor in council, upon the recommendation of the wheat board, may deem to be for the benefit of producers.
This bill is recommended to the house as the continuation of legislation that has enabled western grain to be marketed successfully, and that carries the support of an overwhelming majority of western grain producers.

As the minister has said, the main purpose of the bill is to continue the present system of marketing wheat for another three years. As he has further stated, the great majority of wheat producers in western Canada appear to be in favour of this system of marketing their grain. Under those circumstances I do not think any useful purpose can be served by prolonging unduly the debate concerning this particular method of marketing.
The minister gave a laudatory account of the way in which the wheat board has handled the marketing of grain in the last two or three years, an account in which I think a considerable number of people would not entirely concur. However, on this occasion I do not want to revive arguments we have heard in the house on several occasions in the past concerning the way in which our grain has been handled, the prices secured for it and the losses incurred, estimated at many hundreds of millions of dollars. A large number of people believe that this has resulted from the way the grain was handled.

Do you
believe that?
I certainly believe very large losses were experienced.
Why are you in favour of the bill, then?

As I say, the great majority of farmers in western Canada are in favour of this method of marketing grain. This is a democratic country; and if that is what the majority of producers of wheat want, by way of marketing that wheat, then certainly I am one who is prepared to give it to them.
I think wheat producers would be much better satisfied with the board if its composition were somewhat different. The legislation makes provision for from three to five commissioners. Up to this moment only three have been appointed, and it is the hope of many farm organizations that the other two appointees might be representatives of the wheat producers themselves, so that producer representation on the board might dictate policy to an extent greater than has been the case in the past. I think producer representation to that extent would strengthen the board, and that this suggestion should be followed.

Canadian Wheat Board Act Alternatively the wheat producers have asked tor an advisory board with powers considerably increased over those held by the present so-called advisory board, and that such a body might consist of representatives of the wheat producers. It is the view of the wheat producers that this advisory board should have much greater influence than have any of the producer representatives at the present time with respect to policy decisions.
These are suggested reforms of the wheat board which have been sought for a considerable period of time, and should now be put into effect.
In his speech the minister has given a general account of the amount of wheat marketed and the prices secured for it in the last two or three years. I am sure all hon. members were pleased to hear that as much had been marketed as he indicated, and that prices have held up as well as would appear to have been the case. I am sure, too, that all who are concerned with wheat production will hope that the minister's optimism in respect of the marketing of the present crop is justified. I am not making any predictions in the matter; therefore I am not putting myself in the position of the gentleman whom the minister to some extent castigated during the course of his remarks.
Then I am not particularly clear as to the effect of the section in the bill dealing with unclaimed balances. I have no doubt, however, that we will have a full explanation of how exactly it will work and what disposition will be made of these balances. The bill is somewhat vague in that it says only that these balances shall be disposed of in the interests of the producers as the governor in council may decide. I think we should have some more information on that; but, as I say, perhaps the place to get it is when we are in committee on this bill.

Mr. Speaker, I think all of us from the prairie provinces are glad to know that embedded in our statutes today is the Canadian Wheat Board Act, which has been on the statute books since 1935 and is now to be extended to 1957. Those of us who can look back over the last 30 years on the prairies can remember the long, arduous fight that was put up by the farmers of the prairie provinces to obtain this board, and the controversies that arose in 1935. I remember those controversies very well because I was a new member of the house and took some part in the discussions of those days.
However, I hope that as far as we in western Canada are concerned, those controversies are ended. We have seen this board [Mr. Harkness.l

in operation and we know the benefits that have been conferred upon the people who produce grain. We know that the farmers in the wheat growing industry have achieved something in the nature of stability.
During the course of his remarks the minister gave the details of the quantities of wheat that had been sold through the board over the last year or so. That was indeed a most satisfactory statement. As he said, we shall probably have a large carryover this year which undoubtedly the world needs if ways and means can be found of paying for the wheat and giving our farmers a reasonable return for their labours when the grain is marketed. No one can foretell what the future holds, but it is obvious that the world will need quantities of wheat for a long time to come.
I believe we have been fortunate over the last period of time because there were short crops in Australia and in Argentina, and also rice was not available from Burma and Indochina for India and Japan. That gave us additional markets for our wheat and helped considerably. I hope those countries have acquired a taste for wheat so that we may have markets even though other countries increase their cereal production, and even though our cereal production is maintained or increased, as we all hope it will be.
We may talk about the value of our minerals and our forest products, which I noted the other day have exceeded the value of our agricultural production, at least in the export market; nonetheless grain is still one of the major factors in our economy and one of the foundations of our economic stability. In this country we all hope the farmers will be able through good weather and through the methods they are now using in the production of grain to continue at least this high production, and that the world will find ways and means of taking that production in a manner which will be satisfactory to those who produce the crops.
The minister was not in a position today to say anything about the prospects of renewing the international wheat agreement. I hope an agreement will be reached. I hope the price under that agreement will be satisfactory. As I have said already, we do not know what the next few years will bring. We may have a higher production and other countries like Australia and Argentina may have a higher production. Northern Africa under the French regime may be exporting wheat again, or new lands may be opened up for cereal production. We cannot get any

information regarding the outlook, but we may see wheat available for export from the Soviet union.
We remember how they exported large quantities of wheat and took low prices in the early 1930's. We remember what that did to our market for Canadian wheat. It is often said that the depression in the prairie provinces was due to crop failures. To a large degree it was; but it was also due to the exceedingly low prices obtained for wheat when it was sold on the speculative market without any real attempt at maintaining real stability. In my own constituency farmers hauled their wheat to the market at 19 and 20 cents per bushel at the country elevator. That was ruinous. The wheat board and international agreements have permitted Canada and other producing countries to attempt to give some stability to the market along with a more reasonable return to the producers.
Therefore I hope the international wheat agreement will be renewed. I hope our government will do everything possible to get such an agreement. I hope the consuming nations will realize that our farmers' costs of production have increased drastically over the past five years, and that they will be willing to pay a price which will give our farmers a reasonable return for their labour. Various prices have been named to me by some of my constituents ranging from $2.05 up to $2.35 per bushel. They are most anxious, however, that a reasonable market be assured to them once again through a satisfactory international wheat agreement.
I hope ways and means will be found of achieving a satisfactory agreement and, as far as our country is concerned, of permitting the nations that will buy our wheat to obtain the dollars to pay for that wheat from this country. In other words I would like to see a still further downward revision of our customs duties and tariffs. These tariffs have bedevilled trade as far as our farmers are concerned over a period of years. These are barriers against our own income. They are not just barriers against manufactured goods coming in to compete; they are barriers against the returns which must pay for the things we can produce and need to export.
So I am happy this afternoon to have the opportunity of supporting this bill, and to see that it is the intention to maintain the act until August 1, 1957. When the time approaches for its renewal I feel sure that our farmers will want to see the wheat board act renewed again.
The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) said a few moments ago that undoubtedly the minister would give us some
(58108-217
Canadian Wheat Board Act information with regard to these unclaimed balances when we are in committee on the bill. I should like to say at this stage that as I read this section of the act it gives our farmers some assurance that before any disposition is made of the accumulated surpluses a real attempt will be made to adjust the fund so that those who are entitled under it to payments on certificates will get all that can possibly be paid to them. Then, when that is over, any undistributed balance should be used for the benefit, as it is put here, of producers.
How can these balances be used? Various methods occur to those of us who have thought about this matter in the past. The money might be distributed for the improvement of cereal crops, for assistance in the production of new and better types of wheat. It might be used for agricultural education, particularly in those branches of agriculture that have to do with cereals. In any event, it should be used for the benefit of producers.
That brings me to support a view already expressed by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) with respect to the wheat board. Over the years our farmers have asked for more adequate producer representation on the wheat board, and we have discussed that matter back and forth in the house. It is perfectly true that persons who understand the actual mechanics of the marketing of wheat must be on the board, and in the person of Mr. Mclvor I think we have a man who has been a very good chairman of the board in the past. But our grain producers want more adequate producer representation. It might be wise to consider enlarging the board to seven members, but in any event of the five members now on the board I think two or even three should be directly interested at all times in the production of wheat.
As far as an advisory committee is concerned, that is another way of giving the producers representation; but our farmers would be much more satisfied with the operations of the board and the negotiation of agreements by it if they felt that they were more adequately represented than they have been in the past.
The wheat board act was placed on the statute books after many years of effort on the part of western farmers and those of us who supported them. I remember the period before 1921 when we had a wheat board. I remember the interim period after 1921 when we were without one. I remember the years between 1930 and 1935. I remember the controversy that followed the passage of this act in 1935; but one thing that those of us who come from the prairie provinces and

Canadian Wheat Board Act represent agricultural constituencies can say is that today there is unanimity among prairie representatives in the House of Commons and substantial unanimity on the part of the farmers themselves.
Surely no one wants to go back again to the old open market method, with its dealings in futures and gambling on the grain exchange. In those days farmers hauled in their wheat in the fall, received low prices, and the speculator benefited the following spring. No one wants to return to that situation. The wheat board act has been something of a charter for the western wheat grower, and I am very happy this afternoon to be able to support the bill for its continuance until 1957.

Mr. Speaker, as a representative of western agriculturists I am very glad to see this bill introduced this afternoon. I am not speaking only for myself, because all in this group will give the bill their full support. I can look back a little over 30 years to the time when the first wheat board legislation was introduced, in 1919. I must say that we regretted very much when that legislation was done away with a few years later. As the result of it being done away with, the farmers then got busy and organized the wheat pools. The province of Alberta did the job first, and Saskatchewan and Manitoba followed. I am glad to say that the pools are still doing a good job.
In my opinion the Canadian wheat board, which has been talked about and opposed for many years in certain parts of Manitoba, still continues to do an excellent job. It is doing a good job of selling and a good job of satisfying agriculture as a whole in the western provinces. The handling of the crops of the past two or three years has been referred to by the minister. I can remember quite well that on September 25, 1950, and on the same date in 1951, the weather broke and at that time very little of the crop had been threshed. That brought about particularly tough conditions, and we had a lot of out of condition grain. I am glad to say that the vast majority of the farmers are very well satisfied with the prices that have been obtained for them by the wheat board.
As the minister has pointed out, the 1952 crop is the largest that western Canada has ever grown, and to a very great extent that accounts for the degree of prosperity existing in agriculture at the present time. I am sure, though, that we would have been much better off if certain safeguards had been provided when framing the international wheat agreement. We have pointed out our
[Mr. Coldwell.l

reasons for suggesting that in the past, and I hope some safeguards will be placed in the agreement that is now under discussion. I also hope that in the near future the minister will be able to give us the definite information that an agreement has been concluded. Whether or not an agreement is successfully concluded, I believe we need the wheat board to market our grain. It has done an excellent job in the past; and if an international wheat agreement should not be successfully completed then the board- will be able to carry on and I am sure it will do a good job.
I should like to see this legislation made permanent rather than go out of existence after July 31, 1957. I agree with the minister that it is a good idea to have matters reviewed now and again, but even though the legislation were made permanent such a review could undoubtedly take place. I hope that neither the present minister, as long as he holds his office, nor his successor, whoever he may be, will change their minds about the benefits that accrue to western farmers and Canada as a whole as the result of the operations of the Canadian wheat board. Over the years that the present chairman, Mr. Mclvor, has held his position, I believe he has done a very satisfactory job indeed. That is true not only in his handling of his regular work, but when many of us have had complaints about shortages of box cars and other matters Mr. Mclvor has always been right on the job and has taken immediate and effective action.
I want to pay my compliments to the chief commissioner on this occasion. I believe the closing out of certain accounts will be satisfactory. I am glad to learn that efforts will be made to find the owners of the moneys in those accounts. It is true that many farmers move around quite a bit and do not realize that they have credits in the wheat board account. It is good to see that the moneys will be retained for a certain number of years before being disposed of in some other manner. I also hope that the government will see to it that the moneys are properly spent in the interests of agriculture when these accounts are finally disposed of.
Dealing with our internal wheat policy, I am not yet in agreement with the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I have told him that on several occasions. I cannot see yet any sound reasoning why we subsidize our Canadian people at the expense of the prairie wheat growers.
Hear, hear.

On more than one occasion the minister has stated that he was not going to

have the Canadian taxpayers subsidize the wheat growers of Canada. To get the matter straight, instead of that I would suggest that the Canadian wheat growers, the wheat growers of the prairie provinces, are subsidizing not only the people of Canada but also to a certain extent those of other countries. I say that because certain precautions have not been taken to safeguard the interests of the wheat growers. I have pointed out on different occasions that the cost of production has increased very materially since the contract was made.
At the time the agreement was being entered into we pointed out that these conditions could occur. I believe it was only a week ago today that I pointed out that the index of farm machinery prices has increased by 54 points during the past five years and that freight rates, I believe, have increased by some 87 per cent during the past few years. There is no safeguard there at all; and do not forget that the Canadian farmers, the wheat growers on the prairies, bear the brunt of every one of those freight rate increases.
I have not prepared a speech on this matter and I will not say any more at the present time. We shall perhaps have something to say on the different sections as they are being discussed. I do want to say that we are glad to see this legislation introduced, and we shall give it our full support.

Mr. Chairman, I wonder if the minister would tell us if any consideration has been given recently to filling the five commissioner appointments, as they will now be called, particularly with producer representatives.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would gladly fill the other two vacancies if I could find men as competent as the three men who are on the board at the present time. My hon. friend talks about producer representatives, but I might explain that the purpose of this board is to sell wheat, not to grow it. I suppose we could specialize on the growing end by appointing a producer but I do not see that it would strengthen the selling end very much.
The present members of the board are the same men whom the wheat pools themselves have called upon in the past to sell their wheat. They are all from the sales departments of the wheat pools, the men whom the farmers hire. I think they are the type of 68108-2171
Canadian Wheat Board Act men necessary to handle this enormous business of selling wheat, oats and barley from the prairie provinces.

As the minister well knows, the idea of having representatives of the producers on the board is not for the purpose of producing grain. It is for the purpose of allowing the producers to have a greater hand in determining matters of policy for the selling of grain. The grain belongs in toto to the producers, and theirs are the interests to be served. It would seem reasonable that they should have some representation on the board to help determine policies to be followed in matters of entering into agreements and so forth, as far as the selling end is concerned. I am sure there would not be undue difficulty in getting two men from the ranks of the producers who could serve an extremely useful purpose, men who would have knowledge for selling purposes as well as knowledge of the producers' problems.

I do not think this means that farmers have had any lack of confidence in the men who have been selling our wheat, at all, but I think it is quite important to* have the closest possible co-operation from the producers. If the producers feel that they are more or less directly represented by two producers who understand their problems, they will feel more satisfied with what the board does. Those men, moreover, would be able to report back to other producers of wheat. I think the idea is to keep the closest possible liaison between the board and the producers.
What I, at least, have to say is not implying any criticism of the present board; but in the interests of close co-operation with the producers the board, I think, might include at least two producers.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
I might explain that the selling of wheat is itself a highly technical matter. It takes years of training to know really what the mechanics are. I do not think my hon. friend would suggest that we should have a board of five, three with technical knowledge and two without technical knowledge. The whole board is not always in one location. The international wheat
agreement is an agreement on price, is it not?

speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. 148, to amend the Statistics Act.

subsubtopic: UTILIZATION OF SERVICES OF OFFICERS IN OTHER DEPARTMENTS, ETC.
speechtext: Explain.

speakeroldname: Mr. G. J. Mcllraiih (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: UTILIZATION OF SERVICES OF OFFICERS IN OTHER DEPARTMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this bill does not involve any change in the nature of the work being done by the bureau of statistics; it does not involve any matter of principle in relation to that work. It rather has to do with a number of small changes in the authority of the bureau in respect to certain of the techniques of operation.

It is of a nature that the amending clauses contained in the bill are not directly related one to the other. For that reason it is probably something that could best be discussed in committee, but I should say a word, perhaps, about each of the clauses in the bill.
The first part of clause 1 merely deals with an omission in the act when it was passed in 1948, in that the definition dealing with transportation statistics omitted the term "persons", so the bureau could collect statistics of transportation as to goods but not as to persons. Then there is a change in the language used in the definition of public utility.
Section 3 authorizes the minister to utilize the services of employees of other departments, and in addition the effect of it is to make them subject to the penalty for breach of the secrecy provisions of the act. The necessity for that section comes about in connection with the use of census records under the old age security legislation. It merely authorizes the minister to utilize the services of employees of another department. The effect of that is, of course, as will be seen, to prevent a duplication of work by an employee of the Department of National Health and Welfare and the bureau of statistics.
The next clause has to do with the returns made by hospitals, mental institutions and the like. It permits a lesser degree of secrecy with respect to parts of these returns and the publication of them. The publication of information given by hospitals and other similar non-commercial institutions is of such a nature that it must be related to a particular institution to be valuable. This change meets with the wishes of the institutions and the health and similar authorities supplying and using this information.
Paragraph (c) of that clause permits the publication of the names and locations of firms and their products. Formerly that exception was not made, and there was a question about the right to publish certain trade information. Hon. members will notice that the language used in this paragraph is very narrow; publication is confined to the names and locations of the individual firms and the types of products processed.
The next clause concerns the census of population and agriculture. Under the present section the provisions are absolutely rigid, so that it is necessary for the bureau to include in the census questionnaires information it may already have. The modified language in section 4 permits more flexibility, and should result in the cutting down of questions on census forms.
Statistics Act
Then section 5 in the bill has to do with statistics on inland waterways. Part of those statistics is already authorized, but there is no comprehensive statistical information authorized in respect of inland waterways, and the point is clarified in section 5 of the bill.
Section 6 merely provides that statistics relating to criminal offences will be collected at periods more agreeable to the proper working of the courts and the provincial authorities giving the statistics, rather than on the rigid basis defined in the older legislation.
Sections 7 and 8 have the same effect. They simply change the rigid period for the giving of information concerning criminal statistics, as set out in the old legislation, and make the system more flexible. I understand this meets with the approval of those who will give the information.
There is not much more that could be said usefully on this motion for second reading. It seems to me that the points might more properly be dealt with when we are in the committee stage.

subsubtopic: UTILIZATION OF SERVICES OF OFFICERS IN OTHER DEPARTMENTS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the changes contemplated in this revision of the Statistics Act do not seem to be extensive. I trust they will not produce the effect of piling up more useless statistics, at considerable expense to the people of Canada who have to supply them.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Defence Production; Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: UTILIZATION OF SERVICES OF OFFICERS IN OTHER DEPARTMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
These amendments are
designed to cut down rather to increase.

subsubtopic: UTILIZATION OF SERVICES OF OFFICERS IN OTHER DEPARTMENTS, ETC.
speechtext:
I hope that will be the effect. I have heard a number of complaints from businessmen concerning returns they have to make to the statistics branch. The information I receive in many cases is that the material they have to supply is completely useless.
I have been approached on this matter on numerous occasions, and have a considerable pile of correspondence from what I believe to be the largest distributor of motor car products in western Canada. This organization has had to employ considerable staff, at great expense, to engage in the process of filing these numerous returns. It handles items of equipment and the like. The information I have indicates that this distributor, and one other concern in eastern Canada, are the only people doing this particular kind of business. He believes the statistics he has to turn in are quite valueless; nevertheless he has to keep turning them in year after

Statistics Act
year. If he does not he is subject to the penalties, stated as follows in the act:
Every person who, without lawful excuse, . . .
(b) refuses or neglects to furnish any information or to fill up to the best of his knowledge and belief any schedule or form-
-shall be liable, upon summary conviction, to a penalty not exceeding $100 and not less than $20, or to imprisonment for a period not exceeding three months and not less than thirty days, or to both fine and imprisonment.
It seems to me there should be a bit of housecleaning, so far as the statistics branch is concerned, particularly in the matter of information which is not going to be of any particular value. There seems to have been a great tendency to pile up statistics. It is the sort of thing that snowballs. I am sure there is a great deal of validity in the complaints I have received concerning the statistical information which businessmen must file. I believe the work of the statistics branch and of private business could be speeded up by cutting down much of the useless information now required. I would hope that some effort might be made in that direction.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert H. Winters (Minister of Resources and Development) moved
subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 110, to establish the historic sites and monuments board of Canada.
He said: A famous Nova Scotian and Canadian statesman, Joseph Howe, once said that "a wise nation fosters national pride and love of country by perpetual reference to the sacrifices and glories of the past". One expression of the interest which we Canadians have in the history and tradition of our country is the recognition we have given to the importance of preserving and marking our ancient monuments and historic sites. These things recall not only great moments of the past, but thoughts and doings of other days, different from our own and yet a part of all that we are.
The object of the bill now before the house is to provide for the placing of the historic sites and monuments board of Canada on a statutory basis. Public interest in the board has increased greatly in recent years and more emphasis has been placed on the value of its work. The royal commission on national development in the arts, letters and sciences recommended a more comprehensive program of preserving and marking historic sites and monuments. The reconstitution of the board under the authority of an act of parliament would give fuller recognition to the importance of its function.
It is many years now since the federal government first recognized its responsibilities to honour and preserve this national heritage. The national parks branch, which was established in 1911, administered several historic sites, being primarily interested in scenic preservation. In June 1919, following extended representations from numerous organizations and individuals across Canada, the then minister of the interior nominated

an honorary historic sites and monuments board to advise the department in the selection of sites and events of national historic importance and thus worthy of commemoration. This first board was composed of a chairman, Brigadier General E. A. Cruick-shank, LL.D., F.R.S.C., of Ottawa, and five other recognized authorities on the history of the different parts of Canada. Among the members was the commissioner of the parks branch, who was the officer representing the department of the interior. The board served without remuneration, but the members received an allowance of $10 a day and their ordinary travelling expenses when attending meetings away from their places of residence.
In 1923 the board was reconstituted and the members were appointed by the governor in council. It was provided in the order in council that "the board is honorary, serves without remuneration and acts in an advisory capacity to the Department of the Interior, in regard to the historic sites of national interest". The reconstituted board consisted of seven members, and Brigadier General
E.	A. Cruickshank was appointed to carry on as chairman.
Subsequent orders in council were passed from time to time, adding to the membership of the board and filling vacancies as they occurred. The board is presently composed of thirteen members, including one member from each province; the dominion archivist; a representative from the national parks and historic sites division of the Department of Resources and Development and a retired official of the department. The members of the present board are:
Professor Fred Landon, M.A., LL.D., D.Litt.,
F.	R.S.C., London, Ontario-chairman.
Professor D. C. Harvey, M.A., LL.D., F.R.S.C.,
archivist, the public archives of Nova Scotia, Halifax, Nova Scotia.
The Honourable E. Fabre-Surveyer, LL.M., B.C.L., LL.D., F.R.S.C., the judges' chambers, superior court, Montreal, P.Q.
The Reverend Antoine d'Eschambault, D.S.T., D.J.C., Genthon, Manitoba.
Professor M. H. Long, M.A., F.R.S.C., department of history, the University of Alberta, Edmonton, Alberta.
Walter N. Sage, Esq., M.A., Ph.D., F.R.S.C., F.R. Hist. S., head of department of history, the University of British Columbia, Vancouver, British Columbia.
The Honourable Thane A. Campbell, M.A., LL.D., chief justice of Prince Edward Island, Charlottetown, Prince Edward Island.
W. Kaye Lamb, Esq., M.A., Ph.D., LL.D., F.R.S.C., dominion archivist, public archives of Canada, Ottawa, Ontario.
Charles E. A. Jeffery, Esq., M.B.E., editor, The Evening Telegram, St. John's, Newfoundland.
Alfred G. Bailey, Esq.,.M.A., Ph.D., F.R.S.C., dean of arts, the University of New Brunswick, Fredericton, New Brunswick.
Historic Sites and Monuments
Campbell Innes, Esq., M.A., honorary superintendent, Fort Battleford national historic park, Battleford, Saskatchewan.
W.D. Cromarty, Esq., Ottawa, Ontario.
C.G. Childe, Esq., B.Sc., national parks branch, Ottawa, Ontario.
The board meets each year. In addition to the meetings a considerable amount of work is carried on by correspondence. The work of the board has been increasing and it is possible that in future more than one meeting each year will be necessary.
Hon. members will note that the board's function is advisory only. The implementation of their recommendations is subject to the approval of the minister and to funds being voted by parliament.
Hon. members may ask what criteria can be adopted in deciding whether an historic site is of national interest and significance rather than of only local interest and importance. What the board has done is to recognize certain broad and flexible divisions of Canadian history within which lie events and persons properly of interest to Canadians wherever they may be. These divisions reach back to prehistoric times, which have bequeathed to us relics of Indian life such as are to be found in Ontario and in British Columbia. Then follow the discovery and early exploration of Canada; the earliest French settlements in Quebec and Nova Scotia; the events of the Seven Years war in America; the defence of Canada during the American war of Independence and the war of 1812; the rebellion of 1837 and subsequent "patriot" invasions; the Fenian raids and the uprisings in the northwest in 1870 and 1885; and the exploration of the Canadian west from lake Superior to the Pacific ocean and northward to the Arctic.
In addition to this pageant of our history there are included as well the political development of Canada from the struggle in Nova Scotia for responsible government onward through confederation and the creation of new provinces; the entry into confederation of Newfoundland; our economic development; the social development of the Canadian people; and lastly the achievements of distinguished Canadians both at home and abroad.
Hon. members may be surprised to know that since 1919 the historic sites and monuments board has examined for their historical significance the circumstances surrounding more than one thousand historic sites. It has declared 623 of these sites to be of national importance.
Recommendations by the board, whose functions as I have said are purely advisory, would, under this bill, be submitted to the

Historic Sites and Monuments Minister of Resources and Development. On his approval, appropriate action is taken by the national parks branch, which has the responsibility for marking and preserving historic sites, subject of course to parliament providing the necessary funds. Already 429 historic sites have been marked or acquired. The remainder, together with future additions, will be dealt with as circumstances permit. The extent to which new projects can be undertaken is, of course, necessarily limited to the appropriations made available. In the three fiscal years ending 1952-53, total appropriations for the construction and operating costs of historic sites and national historic parks have averaged some $226,000 annually.
Perhaps I should refer now to the authority under sections 11 and 12 of the National Parks Act for the establishment of national historic parks. These sections provide that the governor in council may set apart any land, the title to which is vested in Her Majesty, as a national historic park to commemorate an historic event of national importance or to preserve any historic landmark or any object of historic, prehistoric or scientific interest of national importance and to bring it under certain provisions of the National Parks Act for administrative purposes. There are now eleven national historic parks in Canada, from the fortress of Louisbourg in the east to the recently acquired Fort Battle-ford in the west, administered by the national parks branch. At the present time certain sites are being considered as national historic parks in our newest province of Newfoundland. On the recommendation of the historic sites and monuments board, important preservative action has been taken in these parks, and several museums established to house important exhibits relating to the early histories of the surrounding districts.
In recent years there seems to be a growing desire in Canada to have commemorated the achievements of distinguished Canadians. Names of such prominent Canadians as Sir John A. Macdonald, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, Mr. W. L. Mackenzie King and others have been established in perpetuity in a variety of ways both in the minds of our citizens as well as in plaque and statue. It may be of interest to hon. members that the board recommended at its meeting in May, 1952 that memorial tablets be erected in honour of the late Viscount Bennett at Calgary, Alberta, and at Hopewell, New Brunswick. Arrangements are under way at the present time to have this recommendation carried out. I might also mention that the board has for consideration at its next meeting the question of suitable commemoration of the birthplace of Sir Robert Laird Borden at Grand Pre, Nova Scotia.


The bill now before the house provides for the establishment of a board of twelve members; ten to be appointed by the governor in council and representing each of the provinces. The other two members would be the dominion archivist and the chief curator of the national museum. The chairman is to be appointed by the governor in council. The appointed members would hold office for periods not exceeding five years and any retiring member may be eligible for reappointment.
The powers and duties of the board as set forth in the bill are to receive and consider recommendations respecting the marking or commemoration of historic sites, the establishment of historic museums and the administration of such places, and to advise the minister in carrying out his duties under the act.
The bill defines an historic place as a site, building or other place of national interest or significance, and power is given to the minister to mark such places and to provide for their care and preservation. Authority is also sought subject to the approval of the governor in council to establish historic museums and to acquire land for such purpose.
I believe that hon. members will regard this bill as a tribute to the outstanding work successive historic sites and monuments boards have done over the years. It recognizes the need for permanency in this important phase of our Canadian growth and development as a nation. As Canadians, we cannot but be impressed by the greatness of the legacy our history has left to us to cherish and preserve. By continuing to work toward our objective of preserving the historic sites, buildings and objects of national interest, we shall be making a significant contribution to the education and inspiration of all our people and of visitors from other lands.

subtopic: ESTABLISHMENT OF BOARD ON STATUTORY BASIS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that all members of the house are interested in and find themselves in sympathy with the statement that has been made by the Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters). As he pointed out, no part of Canada has more historic sites, with only a few of them having been marked, than Nova Scotia. No part of Canada has had more individuals, whose record in the life of Nova Scotia and the life of Canada as a whole is more deserving of commemoration, than the province of Nova Scotia. The minister quoted in his remarks the well known words of Hon. Joseph Howe, one of the great Nova Scotians, with which words we are all in agreement. A great deal could be said about and direct references made to the past and present of Nova Scotia.

The minister referred to two prime ministers of Canada, Sir Robert Borden and Viscount Bennett. There are two other Nova Scotians who also became prime ministers of Canada, Sir John Thompson and Sir Charles Tupper. They were both great Canadians who left their imprint on the life of Canada. I have said before and I repeat that Canada would not be what it is, and perhaps would never have existed as it does today, if it had not been for the work carried on by Sir Charles Tupper in the days of confederation. In my native town of Amherst we had four fathers of confederation, Sir Charles Tupper, Hon. Robert Barry Dickey, great-grandfather of the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Dickey), Hon. Edward Chandler and Hon. Jonathan McCully.

Owing to the labour troubles in the Kootenays in British Columbia at the beginning of this century, the federal government appointed what was called a royal labour commission to investigate the whole situation and former prime minister Mackenzie King, who was then deputy minister of labour, was the secretary of the commission. When that commission reported to the government it recommended the legal prohibition of socialism in Canada, and prohibition of the publication of all socialist literature. Anyway, this clash between the owners and the workers continued, and as a result of the continued organization of the workers the first move was made in Rossland that resulted in labour for the first time in the British commonwealth being able to strike without suffering action for damages.
The first right that labour won was the right to organize; the second right was to strike without the union being sued for damages, and that right was first won in the British commonwealth in the town of Rossland, British Columbia, in my constituency. In that connection I just wish to quote briefly from the Labour Gazette of 1904: An act to amend the law relating to trade unions was passed in British Columbia; and from the Labour Gazette I quote the following:
This act is of extreme importance in trade union history, not only in British Columbia hut also in Canada and the British empire. The statute originated from circumstances similar to those that made necessary the passage of the trade disputes act in Great Britain in 1906, but it will be noted that the provincial statute was passed four years earlier. From July to November, 1901, about one thousand miners at Rossland, organized as a local of the western federation of miners, struck for higher wages and union recognition by the Le Roi Mining Company. In October the company sued the union for damages and asked for an injunction to restrain local unions for attempting to persuade

others not to work for the company; the company was particularly annoyed when members of the union succeeded in getting imported strikebreakers to cease work. The courts awarded $12,500 and costs to the company and a receivership was established. Following this decision in British Columbia protests were made regarding the law relating to trade unions as they were later in Britain following the Taff Vale decision. Martin's legislation was a direct response to these protests and in general provided simply that no trade union was to be liable in damages for any wrongful act in connection with a labour dispute unless such act had been authorized or concurred in by the members of the union or by its officers acting within their powers under the rules of the union.
Now, Mr. Speaker, that was an event of international significance. I again suggest to the minister that the place where for the first time in the British commonwealth a trade union won the right to strike without being liable to damages is a place where a significant social event occurred and justifies recognition by the historic sites and monuments board.

Mr. Speaker, as Nova Scotia is steeped in history I should like to take a few moments to speak in this debate. The Minister of Resources and Development (Mr. Winters) and the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) have mentioned Joseph Howe. I was very glad to hear his name mentioned, as indeed I am at all times, for about the time of confederation that great Nova Scotian, who fought and obtained responsible government for Nova Scotia and thus for the rest of Canada, said that a wise nation preserves its records, gathers up its muniments, decorates the tombs of its illustrious dead, repairs its great public structures and fosters national pride and love of country by perpetual reference to the sacrifices and glories of the past.
I suggest that the works Joseph Howe advocated and revered are being carried out efficiently and well in all ten provinces of Canada by the minister. He is following the precepts of Joseph Howe; he is conscious that sites and monuments must be preserved for posterity and that our great men of history must be honoured.
Mr. Speaker, we from the bluenose country are very proud of our history and the part played by our forefathers in the development of Canada. Nova Scotia has the proud distinction of being the only province of Canada and the first colony of Great Britain to possess, through royal charter, a flag of its own. The flag of Nova Scotia traces its origin to the charter of New Scotland granted in 1621 to Sir William Alexander, afterwards the Earl of Stirling, by King James VI of Scotland and I of England.
And here, sir, may I say that we have no desire to flaunt this flag; for I believe, Mr. Speaker, that there is one flag for Canada, not ten; as far as I am concerned personally that good old historic flag, the union jack, is adequate. Indeed, we do ourselves honour thereby. Our people must possess a full appreciation of our history; they must place a value on the links with the past. Too many of these links have already been lost through sheer neglect-to cite only one, the routes of the early explorers.
What appeals to me, sir, and I am sure it must also strike every hon. member in this 

house, is the fact that all provinces of Canada are receiving equal attention from the Department of Resources and Development; no one part is favoured. I am sure, if I might be permitted to speak for Nova Scotia, I could name many parts of the province that have had suitable monuments erected or parks opened in commemoration of some great historic event. May I mention only a few: Shelburne, the Loyalist town; Louisburg and her forts; Wolfe's Landing; King's College, the oldest university in the Queen's overseas dominions, or rather in the British commonwealth as it is known today. Then there is Liverpool, Nova Scotia; Lunenburg, the home of the minister; Annapolis, the home of the "Firsts" in Canada, and where Champlain built his first trading post. And I must not overlook Halifax and Dartmouth, two places full of history which are very well monu-mented and marked by the historic sites board. For this we are very grateful to the minister for his co-operation and consideration.
Among the places suitably marked in Halifax are: The site of the first printing press in Canada; a plaque in commemoration of the battle between the Shannon and the Chesapeake, when the Shannon defeated a very brave foe and towed her into Halifax; the site of the first post office in Canada; a monument erected on the grounds of Dalhousie university known as the Castine cairn, erected to commemorate an expedition of combined forces of the army and navy, when it invaded Maine and captured Machias. A customs office was set up; and if the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann) were in his seat tonight he would be interested to know that they collected this money, brought it back to Canada and established a university.
Then there is the site of the first zoo in North America; a monument to Captain Samuel Cook, the world explorer once stationed in Halifax; and there are many other things. But all attainments are climaxed by the minister's department taking over the rehabilitation of historic Citadel hill, Fort St. George, and the old town clock, saving them for posterity. Both of these were built by the Duke of Kent, the father of Queen Victoria. The fort gets its name from the duke's father, King George III.
In this connection I wish to refer to the invaluable contribution to these developments by our Nova Scotia archivist, Dr. D. C. Harvey. board. His work is best summed up in the words "modesty and integrity", qualities which arise, in part, from a keen historical sense and which all citizens would do well to emulate. That figure would not perhaps impress those from eastern Canada very greatly, but 75 years back, nearly a hundred years back, there was nothing at all in western Canada except Indian tribes.

Fort Macleod was known in those days and established as an outpost by what was then the North West Mounted Police. The town of Macleod, from which the constituency which I have the honour to represent is named, was in the early days known as Fort Macleod. Eventually the post office there became known as Macleod, and it was so indicated in the post office guide.
In the early days that fort was a landmark in the southern part of Alberta and the post of the historic North West Mounted Police. I am reminded by my leader here that Fort Macleod of that area was for many years the only outpost of the North West Mounted Police west of Regina. It was largely because of the establishment of Fort Macleod in southern Alberta that law and order was brought to western Canada, at least to the regions beyond Regina.
The old barracks of the North West Mounted Police stood for many years in the town of Macleod, but one by one they were allowed to deteriorate until today there is not much of the original buildings left standing. I believe it is a shame that this fort with all its historic significance was allowed to deteriorate. Had this present measure been effective right along throughout the years perhaps these buildings would not have been allowed to deteriorate and almost completely disappear.
I therefore welcome this measure and ask the minister to exercise his authority under it, as will many other hon. members for certain sites in their own constituencies. I believe that Fort Macleod in southern Alberta has a sort of priority in claim to be restored and for suitable monuments to be placed there. Many books have been written about the experiences and the life of the people in that part of the country in the early days.
I might mention this, Mr. Speaker, in connection with what was said by the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray). He assumed that the fort was moved. That is not so. What happened was simply this. Interested and civic-minded citizens of the town of Macleod, seeing what was happening in respect to the old fort, wanted to call a halt to it. Recognizing that the town of Macleod had a historic background, they desired only to restore the original name, and they took appropriate action. Today that town is now known as the town of Fort Macleod. I believe it will now become necessary to amend even the Canada Elections Act to have the constituency known as the constituency of Fort Macleod. That is desirable, in any event.

I might say this. Perhaps I am a bit rusty on my western Canada geography, but quite frankly I may say that I did not know there was a post office named Fort McLeod away up in the Cariboo country until the name of the town of Macleod in southern Alberta was restored to its original name of Fort Macleod. The only thing that has happened is that the town of Macleod has now reverted to its original name of Fort Macleod. It does have a history, and an exceedingly important one. I ask the minister to take this fact into account when he exercises his authority under this particular measure.

As the Massey commission points out, the national museum will be concerned with such matters as geology, botany, zoology and natural history, all of which have nothing particularly to do with historic sites and monuments. I shall not deal further with that point.
My second comment is that the Massey commission recommended that two members of this board be nominated by the Canadian historical association, and I quote from page 348 of the report as follows:
Two members to be nominated by the council of the Canadian historical association, similarly for five-year terms and similarly eligible for reappointment for one further term.
I think there is a great deal of merit in that recommendation, for several reasons. The present and future members of the board may be either professional historians, if I may use that term, or amateur historians, as are many members of the House of Commons. They may very well be people who are keenly interested in the history of Canada. On the other hand, from time to time the membership of the board may comprise those who have not an adequate knowledge of the history of Canada, such as obviously is in the possession of the members of the council of the Canadian historical association. I think it would be most useful to have, as has been suggested, two members of that association appointed to this board. It would have value in that you would have on the board competent and trained historians. It would have value in that the Canadian historical association would have a continuing interest in the functioning of the board, and at its annual meetings or on other occasions would presumably have reports from the members of this board and would give close attention to what the historic sites and monuments board was doing.
I think it is in the general interest of this board and of Canadians that there should be wide interest throughout Canada in the work of this historic sites and monuments board, and that can be provided by members of the council of the Canadian historical association who are trained historians and have a background connected with this work.
I would imagine that if it were given the privilege to do so, this organization would from time to time appoint to the board men of outstanding qualities and with special interest in historic sites and monuments. Those are the two things I wanted to draw to the attention of the minister and I would appreciate his comments.
